<reason>Both sides agreed early that life-extension is cheap, and A leveraged that concession relentlessly with a real-world counterfactual (Germany) that B never directly rebutted. But the motion explicitly includes "new-build programs," and B's sustained attack on that pillar—citing the well-known Vogtle/Hinkley/Flamanville overrun pattern—was never answered with an actual per-ton price or a credible Western counterexample. B's pointed pressure question (name one on-time, on-budget Western nuclear build) exposed this directly, and A's answer evaded by pivoting to refurbishment (Darlington) and to renewables' own struggles rather than naming one, effectively conceding the point. B also offered the more analytically responsive frame: life-extension's pool is fixed and finite, so an "equivalent scale-up" comparable to a decade of renewable buildout would necessarily pull in the weak new-build track record, dragging down the blended per-dollar ledger. A never fully closed this gap with hard magnitude comparisons. B's modularity argument (parallel, independently-permitted projects vs. single mega-projects where one delay eats a decade) also gave a sharper structural answer to A's queue-delay complaint than A's rebuttal offered in return. On balance, B's rebuttals were more targeted and did more damage to A's weakest pillar, while A's strongest asset (the life-extension concession) was contained, if not fully neutralized, by the scalability critique.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question (B3.2) asking A to name a Western democracy that delivered new nuclear on original budget/schedule, and A's evasive non-answer in A4.3 (pivoting to refurbishment and offshore wind rather than naming one), which functionally conceded B's core attack on the new-build pillar of PRO's case.</best_rebuttal>
